provenance.route: 1 Corinthians 3:19, via Mosiah 24:7 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “The wisdom of this world” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, 1 Corinthians 1:20, 2:6 and 3:19, and nowhere else; “the wisdom of the world” occurs in no KJV verse, so the Book of Mormon has dropped Paul's demonstrative in both of its uses of the formula. Alma 2:1's is the second, after Mosiah 24:7.
provenance.significance: 1 Corinthians 3:19 does not stop at calling the world's wisdom foolishness. It goes on: 'For it is written, He taketh the wise in their own craftiness' — the KJV's rendering of Job 5:13. Alma 2:1 introduces Amlici as 'a very cunning man, yea, a wise man, as to the wisdom of the world', and the chapter then takes him in his own craftiness: the cunning that draws away much people gets him made king by his own faction, marched against his brethren, and killed in single combat by the judge he tried to replace. The unstated half of the borrowed phrase is the sentence that predicts the plot.

2:1.note: 'He being a very cunning man, yea, a wise man, as to the wisdom of the world.' Paul's phrase, used as a verdict rather than a description, exactly as Mosiah 24:7 used it of the Lamanites — 'a cunning and a wise people, as to the wisdom of the world'. This is a new book and a new subject, an individual rather than a nation, but the formula is identical down to the 'as to' that does the disqualifying, and it is Alma 2's first characterisation of the man the chapter exists to bury. Recorded as a fresh link rather than a recurrence for the reason ADJUDICATING §4 gives for book boundaries.
2:1.text: For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written, He taketh the wise in their own craftiness.

provenance.other: “Drew away much people after him” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 5:37, and the shorter “much people after him” occurs in exactly one, the same verse. Alma 2:2 has 'drawn away much people after him' — five consecutive words, with only the participle changed. The corpus's other borrowing from this family is Acts 20:30's “draw away disciples” (also a KJV singleton), adjudicated at Mosiah 29:7.
provenance.significance: Gamaliel's speech is a test, and Alma 2 applies it. Acts 5:36-39 offers two precedents — Theudas, 'who was slain; and all, as many as obeyed him, were scattered', and Judas of Galilee, who 'drew away much people after him: he also perished; and all, even as many as obeyed him, were dispersed' — and draws the rule: 'if this counsel or this work be of men, it will come to nought: but if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it.' Alma 2 narrates the borrowed clause's own sequel. Amlici draws away much people after him (2:2), is slain by Alma with the sword (2:31), and his followers are scattered and driven into the wilderness (2:37) — slain, scattered, come to nought, in Gamaliel's order. The chapter does not cite the rule; it borrows the example and then supplies the outcome the example was quoted to establish.
provenance.alternative: Acts 20:30, the other KJV singleton in this family, which the corpus has already used at Mosiah 29:7.

2:2.note: Five consecutive words of a KJV singleton, altered only in the tense of the verb. What earns the row beyond the run is that Mosiah 29:7 predicted this event in the *other* singleton — 'draw away a part of this people after him', which is Acts 20:30's construction — and Alma 2:2 reports it in Gamaliel's. The warning is Paul's and the fulfilment is Luke's, and the two are two verses apart in the KJV's own vocabulary for schism. Far below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his thirty-six; recorded as a quotation on the strength of the singleton rather than the length.
2:2.text: After this man rose up Judas of Galilee in the days of the taxing, and drew away much people after him: he also perished; and all, even as many as obeyed him, were dispersed.

provenance.other: “Voice of the people” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 8:7, God's concession to Samuel: 'Hearken unto the voice of the people in all that they say unto thee: for they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me.' Alma 2 uses the phrase four times in five verses (2:3, 2:4, 2:6, 2:7).
provenance.significance: The phrase reverses direction here, and that is the finding. In 1 Samuel 8 the voice of the people is a demand for a king and God grants it as a rejection of himself; at Mosiah 29:2 it was that demand almost verbatim, a people asking an ageing ruler for a king out of his own sons. At Alma 2:7 the same phrase refuses one: 'the voice of the people came against Amlici, that he was not made king over the people.' Two chapters after Mosiah abolished the monarchy on the argument that the voice of the people rarely desires what is wrong, the institution he built out of Israel's worst decision makes the opposite decision in Israel's own words. The unstated correspondence is that 1 Samuel 8 supplies both the mechanism and the warning, and Alma 2:9 immediately shows the warning was sound: the losing faction consecrates Amlici king anyway.
provenance.alternative: 1 Samuel 8:19-20, where the people refuse Samuel's voice and insist on a king 'like all the nations', which is closer to what Amlici's faction then does at 2:9.

2:7.note: 'The voice of the people came against Amlici, that he was not made king over the people.' A KJV singleton, and the corpus's fourth substantial use of it — 2 Nephi 10:11, Mosiah 7:9, Mosiah 29:2 — but the first in which it decides a question the other way. Written in full rather than recorded as a recurrence for both of ADJUDICATING §4's reasons: this is a new book, and the second use is itself the argument, since the passage the phrase first translated is the passage now being answered.
2:7.text: And the LORD said unto Samuel, Hearken unto the voice of the people in all that they say unto thee: for they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them.

provenance.other: “Our wives and our children” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Numbers 14:3 — 'that our wives and our children should be a prey'. The Book of Mormon has 'our fathers, and our wives, and our children be slain'. The surrounding scene is Numbers 13's as well: spies sent to view a land (13:2, 13:17), a return with a report of 'men of a great stature' (13:32), and a night of weeping.
provenance.significance: This is the KJV's spy-report scene, and the Book of Mormon corrects it. In Numbers the returning spies bring 'an evil report' and the people's cry about their wives and children is the faithless sentence that costs Israel forty years and a generation. In Alma 2 the spies are named (2:22), their report is true, and the cry is an accurate alarm that produces the right action: the camp breaks, crosses Sidon, prays, and wins. The unstated correspondence is the verdict Numbers 14 pronounces on the sentence Alma 2:25 borrows — and the difference is not the report but what the hearers do next. Numbers 14:3 ends 'were it not better for us to return into Egypt?'; Alma 2:26 has the people go towards their city instead.
provenance.alternative: 2 Chronicles 20:13's 'their little ones, their wives, and their children', where Judah stands before the LORD before a battle against a great multitude — thematically nearer to Alma 2:28's prayer, but its possessive is third-person and it is not a spy report.

2:25.note: 'Our fathers, and our wives, and our children be slain.' A KJV singleton phrase arriving inside a reproduction of the scene it belongs to: spies sent out (2:21), spies named (2:22), spies returning in fear on the morrow (2:23), a report of a numerous host seen with 'great astonishment' (2:24), then the cry for the wives and the children. The machine ranked Numbers 14:3 on the shared run without seeing the type-scene around it.
2:25.text: And wherefore hath the LORD brought us unto this land, to fall by the sword, that our wives and our children should be a prey? were it not better for us to return into Egypt?

provenance.other: “As the sand” occurs in exactly 18 KJV verses; the simile is common and no single verse owns it. Three of the eighteen apply it to an enemy army — Judges 7:12 (the Midianites, 'as the sand by the sea side for multitude'), Joshua 11:4 and 1 Samuel 13:5 — and one, Genesis 22:17, is the promise to Abraham's seed. The Book of Mormon's 'the sands of the sea' matches no KJV verse exactly.
provenance.significance: Seven verses earlier the narrator stopped the battle to explain a place-name: the army pitches 'in the valley of Gideon, the valley being called after that Gideon which was slain by the hand of Nehor' (2:20). The KJV has one Gideon and one valley, and in that valley the enemy lie 'as the sand by the sea side for multitude' (Judges 7:12) and are beaten by three hundred men, precisely so that Israel cannot 'vaunt themselves against me, saying, Mine own hand hath saved me' (7:2). Alma 2:27-28 has the sand-multitude come up out of the valley of Gideon's camp, and its next sentence gives the victory to the hand of the Lord rather than to numbers. The further recovery is uglier and is the reason the row is worth writing: Genesis 22:17 made the sand of the sea a promise about Abraham's seed, and the sand-multitude here is the Lamanites, who are that seed.
provenance.alternative: A stock biblical simile for an innumerable host, used without reference to any one verse.

2:27.note: 'Being as numerous almost, as it were, as the sands of the sea.' The simile is common and the row does not rest on it. It rests on the narrator having just named the ground after Gideon and explained the name, three verses before deploying the simile that the KJV's Gideon narrative uses for the enemy he faced in a valley. Filed as conceptual and at moderate for that reason.
2:27.whyNot: 'As the sand' is one of the KJV's most widely distributed similes and the Book of Mormon uses it elsewhere without a Judges context. The valley of Gideon is named for a Nephite Gideon, not for the judge, and the text says so explicitly at 2:20 — which cuts both ways, since it shows the narrator thinking about the name at exactly this point.
2:27.text: And the Midianites and the Amalekites and all the children of the east lay along in the valley like grasshoppers for multitude; and their camels were without number, as the sand by the sea side for multitude.

provenance.other: “Out of the hand of their enemies” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Judges 2:18 and Nehemiah 9:27, and both are statements of the judges cycle; the Book of Mormon's plural 'out of the hands of their enemies' occurs in none. “Heard their cry” occurs in exactly three (Exodus 3:7, Nehemiah 5:6, Psalm 106:44). The machine ranked Judges 2:14, the same passage's opposite half — Israel sold 'into the hands of their enemies'.
provenance.significance: Judges 2:11-19 is the KJV's programmatic statement of what a judge is for: the people are sold into the hand of their enemies, they cry, the LORD raises up judges, and he 'delivered them out of the hand of their enemies all the days of the judge'. Alma 2 is the first war of a nation that has just replaced its kings with judges, fought by a chief judge in person, and it resolves in that formula's terms — a cry, a hand, a deliverance. Nehemiah 9:27 states the same cycle retrospectively and adds the word Alma 2:28 needs: 'when they cried unto thee, thou heardest them from heaven … thou gavest them saviours, who saved them out of the hand of their enemies.' What the Book of Mormon does not take from Judges 2 is its last clause, that the people relapsed as soon as the judge died — and Alma 4 will supply it.

2:28.note: 'Having prayed mightily to him that he would deliver them out of the hands of their enemies; therefore the Lord did hear their cries.' No clause is reproduced; two KJV rarities are, and they belong to the passage that defines the office Alma holds. Filed at moderate as conceptual because the deliverance formula is spread widely enough across the KJV that no single verse is compelled.
2:28.whyNot: Deliverance from the hand of enemies is among the KJV's commonest theological sentences and the Book of Mormon has used versions of it since 1 Nephi. The plural 'hands' matches no KJV verse, and the argument depends on the reader granting that the reign of the judges makes Judges 2 relevant.
2:28.text: And when the LORD raised them up judges, then the LORD was with the judge, and delivered them out of the hand of their enemies all the days of the judge: for it repented the LORD because of their groanings by reason of them that oppressed them and vexed them.

provenance.other: “To save your lives” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 45:7, and “to preserve life” occurs in exactly one, Genesis 45:5. Alma 2:30 has 'to save and preserve this people' — both of Joseph's verbs, in Joseph's order, with 'this people' for the lives and the posterity. The pairing is nearly confined in the KJV to this one speech; Genesis 50:20 restates it as 'to save much people alive'.
provenance.significance: Joseph's disclosure to his brothers is the KJV's one place where a man asks to be understood as God's means of preserving his own kindred from destruction — 'God did send me before you to preserve life' — and the brothers he says it to are the ones who sold him. Alma prays it in the middle of single combat against a man whose army is his own people's brethren, and the corpus has used the same speech twice before: 2 Nephi 3:16 makes it a promise about Joseph's seed, and 1 Nephi 5:14 reaches it through Stephen. What Alma adds is the instrument. He does not ask to be preserved; he asks to be 'an instrument in thy hands', which is the phrase Alma 1:8 used of the Gideon whose valley he has just camped in and whose killer's heir he is now fighting.

2:30.note: 'O Lord, have mercy and spare my life, that I may be an instrument in thy hands, to save and preserve this people.' Two KJV singletons from one speech, reduced to their verbs. Filed at moderate rather than high because both verbs are ordinary English and only their pairing is rare; the corpus's earlier use of the same speech at 2 Nephi 3:16 was filed at moderate for the same reason.
2:30.whyNot: 'Save' and 'preserve' are common words and a prayer for a people's deliverance could reach them without Genesis. Nothing else in Alma 2 is Josephan, and the Joseph-in-Egypt frame the corpus uses elsewhere is not invoked here.
2:30.text: And God sent me before you to preserve you a posterity in the earth, and to save your lives by a great deliverance.

provenance.other: “Ravenous birds” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ezekiel 39:4, and “ravenous beast” occurs in exactly one, Isaiah 35:9; the Book of Mormon's plural 'ravenous beasts' occurs in neither. “To be devoured” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, of which Ezekiel 39:4 is one. “Man's bone” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ezekiel 39:15. “Vulture” occurs in exactly three KJV verses (Leviticus 11:14, Deuteronomy 14:13, Job 28:7), none of them a battlefield: the KJV's carrion birds are always 'fowls of the air'.
provenance.significance: Ezekiel 39 is the KJV's one extended account of what becomes of a defeated multitude's bodies, and Alma 2:37-38 uses it in sequence. Ezekiel gives Gog's host 'unto the ravenous birds of every sort, and to the beasts of the field to be devoured' (39:4); the Book of Mormon splits that pair, moves the adjective onto the beasts — 'wild and ravenous beasts' at 2:37 — and supplies a bird of its own, the vulture, which the KJV never uses this way. Ezekiel then spends 39:11-15 on the bones: a valley of burial, seven months of searching, and a man who sets up a sign wherever he sees a bone. Alma 2:38 ends 'their bones have been found, and have been heaped up on the earth' — found and left unburied, which is the one thing Ezekiel's chapter exists to prevent. The suppressed correspondence is a refusal: Ezekiel's slaughter is cleansed from the land and Amlici's is not.

2:38.note: 'Many died in the wilderness of their wounds, and were devoured by those beasts, and also the vultures of the air; and their bones have been found, and have been heaped up on the earth.' No clause is reproduced, but three of the passage's terms are KJV rarities and one of them, 'ravenous', is a singleton that has been moved from the birds to the beasts in the preceding verse. 'Vultures of the air' is the KJV's 'fowls of the air' formula with a word substituted that the KJV uses only in dietary lists — a departure worth recording as such.
2:38.text: Thou shalt fall upon the mountains of Israel, thou, and all thy bands, and the people that is with thee: I will give thee unto the ravenous birds of every sort, and to the beasts of the field to be devoured.
